With this definition of "improper governmental activity," concerns raised earlier by groups such as the California County Counsels Association and the California Association of Sanitation Agencies have been addressed. However, the Attorney General is still concerned about the potential harmful effect of allowing disclosure of what would otherwise be privileged information between attorney and client under the aegis of "improper governmental activity." The definition of the phrase (which earlier included phrases drawn from Rule 3-600, such as "a violation of law reasonably imputable to the organization"), the Attorney General argues, leaves the interpretation of what is improper governmental activity to the individual attorney and his or her personal and political views. "While we may all agree that certain conduct, such as the Quackenbush mis-administration (sic) of the Department of Insurance, should see the light of day, we may have legitimate differences of opinion about whether a governmental activity is "likely to result in substantial injury to the organization," involves "willful misuse of public funds" or "breach of fiduciary duty," or involves the "willful omission to perform" an official duty. The proposed exceptions?will unwisely empower attorneys representing public agencies to act as free agents subject to their personal viewpoint, and place them in a state of perpetual conflict with their clients, chilling the trust and open access to information essential to their profession and compromising their effectiveness." [Letter from the Attorney General's Office, dated June 27, 2002.] The Attorney General suggests limiting the definition of "improper governmental activity" to "conduct that constitutes or would constitute a felony." With this definition, the AG states, there would be little difference between attorneys in interpretation of conduct that should clearly be reported. The Attorney General makes a good point. A broad definition might embolden publicity-seeking disclosures by loose cannons, to the detriment of the government agency. However, their suggested amendment may narrow the bill too much. For example, it is not clear if an agency official who used a government charge card to purchase a personal item during official travel is guilty of a felony. A possible consequence of that narrow amendment is a spate of future legislative measures to upgrade current misdemeanors to felonies, just to protect the government attorney whistleblower. There are other phrases used in the Government Code that also may be used to limit these exceptions to the attorney-client confidentiality rule, such as conduct that is "willful or corrupt misconduct in office" that would be grounds for removal of a public official from office. [Government Code Section 3060 et seq.] This phrase has been extensively interpreted in case law to apply to situations that would appear to be "improper governmental activity" as defined by , although the situations are limited to local agency officials, including school district officials. has been amended to remove from the definition of "improper governmental activity" undefined violations of law "reasonably imputable to the organization" or "likely to cause substantial injury to the organization," which, under Rule 3-600, could trigger an attorney representing an organization to take actions consistent with Section 6068(e) or, if necessary, resign. Thus "improper government activity" includes conduct that is less definitive than a felony, as the Attorney General would prefer, but would fall under "willful or corrupt misconduct in office," "willful or breach of fiduciary duty," "willful misuse of public funds," and conduct constituting "crime, fraud, or serious and willful violations of law." In all of the above cases, the improper governmental activity should probably be tied to substantial harm to the public interest, so that the attorney would be compelled to take the protected actions in order to prevent or rectify the improper governmental activity. First order of action: urge reconsideration and/or go to highest internal authority Under this bill, an attorney who learns of improper governmental activity in the course of representing a governmental organization may take one or both actions specified by Rule 3-600 (B)(1) [urge reconsideration of the matter while explaining its likely consequences to the organization] and (2) [refer the matter to the highest internal authority if warranted]. These actions would be subject to the Section 6068(e) rule of confidentiality, as they are under current law. By specifying the actions that an attorney may take when he or she learns of improper governmental activity, establishes a clear path of action for the attorney to take, rather than a broad spectrum of undefined actions that could be proper under Rule 3-600 (those actions that are "in the best, lawful interest of the organization"). Anthem Blue Cross (Anthem) states that this bill sets up an Exchange framework that is inconsistent with the concept of consumer choice by requiring the exchange to "determine health benefits." Furthermore, Anthem states that the PPACA already establishes benefit tiers and "essential health benefits" for the individual and small employer markets, whether coverage is purchased inside or outside the Exchange, and that having the Exchange "determine and approve benefit designs" is duplicative of federal requirements and will only serve to further limit consumer choice. Anthem writes that this bill makes the Exchange an "active purchaser," thus allowing it to set prices. Anthem states that the PPACA already establishes a rate review process for premiums charged in the individual and small group markets, which will be executed by the CDI and DMHC. Anthem states that if both the regulators and the Exchange are responsible for approving rates without a consistent process, the rates for the same product could be different inside and outside of the Exchange, violating the federal requirement that the entire market be treated as a single risk pool. Finally, Anthem asserts that setting rates in the Exchange would likely politicize the rate- setting process, which has proven to lead to insurer insolvency and insurers withdrawing from the market, reducing choices for consumers. Anthem suggests amending this bill to remove these provisions and instead clarifying that regulation of health plan and insurance products sold through the exchange are the sole purview of the CDI and DMHC. The Association of California Life and Health Insurance Companies (ACLHIC) writes that the Exchange appears to have the power to negotiate rates for the products sold within the Exchange, and at the same time, requires participating carriers to offer the same products outside the Exchange. ACLHIC is concerned that these negotiated rates may not be actuarially sound and place participating carriers at a market disadvantage with nonparticipating carriers. ACLHIC states that participating carriers should compete on quality and price. ACLHIC also writes that there is already extensive criteria for carrier certification to participate in an Exchange included in PPACA, and will be further expanded when federal rules come forward, and that additional and potentially conflicting state standards may serve to limit the choice of plan in the Exchange. ACLHIC argues that, given the robust certification criteria that will already apply, any carrier that can meet those criteria should be eligible to participate in the Exchange. The California Hospital Association (CHA) is concerned over the provision in this bill that specifically expand the role of County Organized Health Systems beyond the original scope and purpose. Compline provides this information in a user-friendly, electronic format on a subscription basis to hundreds of insurance agents and brokers in California. As existing law does not provide for information service companies to have direct access to ex-mod information gathered by the WCIRB, Compline's current source of ex-mod information is through admitted workers' compensation insurers. These insurers are statutorily required to share information on their policyholders with the WCIRB, and, in turn, they can access, in hard copy, WCIRB's consolidated statewide data concerning employer ex-mods and related information. The sponsors state that this bill is necessary in light of plans by the WCIRB to institute a new, on-line system that will allow the WCIRB to provide information, including ex-mod information, electronically to member insurers and agents and brokers who subscribe to the system. This new system is very similar to the system that information service companies currently have in place. The sponsors argue that unless information service companies, such as Compline, can obtain the same information, in the same format and at the same time as the WCIRB intends to release it, information service companies will be unable to compete. The result, sponsors contend, will be that the WCIRB, a quasi-public entity created to collect, compile and analyze data required to be submitted to it from every admitted workers' compensation insurer, will be the exclusive provider of ex-mod information and other related information. The sponsors assert that establishing the WCIRB as the sole provider of this information was not the Legislature's intent, nor was it their intent to allow the WCIRB to develop an exclusive for-profit franchise to sell information to workers' compensation insurance agents and brokers. The sponsors argue that this bill will maintain a competitive market in the business of providing access to workers' compensation ex-mod and other related information, which is used by insurance agents and brokers to facilitate the placement of workers' compensation insurance on behalf of their clients. Without this legislation, the sponsors assert that competition in providing access to this information will be drastically reduced or eliminated

column1: Injury and death by firearm are consistently the most common method of suicide both in the United States and in California, accounting for nearly half of suicides committed. According to the California Department of Public Health (CDPH), self-inflicted injury and suicide by firearm accounted for 4.1 deaths per 100,000 residents in 2017. The use of firearm for self-inflicted injury and suicide result in lethal outcomes in nearly every instance. Further, rates of suicide vary significantly throughout California, both demographically and geographically. Northern rural California residents are significantly more likely to commit suicide than urban or suburban residents, and rates of suicide among older men were nearly five times as high as the rate for all age groups between 1999 and 2016. Suicide by firearm among California men is also consistently higher than women. White and Native American Californians were also found to commit suicide by firearm at disproportionately higher rates than other racial and ethnic groups. When Governor Davis vetoed this proposal contained in AB 527 in 1999, he stated: The current operation of the grand jury, which follows English common law practice, has remained essentially unchanged since California was admitted to the Union in 1850 and has served us well for 150 years... Thus, any major departures from existing practice warrants thorough and thoughtful consideration and debate within the legal community and among legal scholars. In response to the governor's veto, legal scholars at the "Capital Center" noted above conducted a study on the potential reform of California's grand jury system. (Vitiello & Kelso, Reform of California's Grand Jury System, supra at 515.) At the conclusion of its study the Capital Center observed (supportive of the merits of this provision in the measure): Counsel has a role in assuring that a target makes proper invocation of such [constitutional] rights and privileges. Counsel may also encourage some targets to testify. This offers the grand jury a fuller understanding of the facts than might otherwise have been available. The end result increases the grand jury's ability to exercise independent judgment on whether to indict. . . . [T]he creation of the right to counsel furthers independence of the grand jury and . . . serves the public's interest, and not merely the interest of the target. Additionally, twenty years prior to Governor Davis' veto of AB 527 the American Bar Association (ABA) conducted an investigation of the grand jury system, concluding after several years of study that "a witness before the grand jury shall have the right to be accompanied by counsel in his or her appearance before the grand jury." (American Bar Association, Grand Jury Policy and Model Act (1977-1982) (Marcia Christensen ed., 2d ed. 1982) [hereinafter ABA Report].) The ABA commented that limiting the role of counsel would prevent the grand jury from becoming a "mini-trial," but would address concerns about the unfairness of disallowing a witness from being accompanied by counsel. The ABA study went on to observe: Requiring a witness who needs advice of counsel to consult his attorney outside the grand jury room door is awkward and prejudicial. It unnecessarily prolongs the grand jury proceedings and places the witness in an unfavorable light before the grand jurors. The American Law Institute has called it a "degrading and irrational" procedure. It is extremely damaging to the witness continually to get up, go outside, and consult with counsel. This sentiment was reflected in the testimony of former Watergate Special Prosecutor Charles Ruff when he testified before the House Judiciary Subcommittee in 1977, declaring: The mere possibility of occasional disruption simply cannot overcome the right of the individual witness to consult his attorney without going through the mildly absurd process of leaving the grand jury room every time. Indeed, most prosecutors would admit, I think, that they count on the burden of leaving the room to dissuade the witness from asserting his right to counsel." (Testimony before House Judiciary Subcommittee, April 27, 1977, at 3.) Allowing Witnesses to Have an Attorney Present During Grand Jury Testimony Would Put California In Line with the Practices of Other States: A state- by-state study conducted by the United States Department of Justice, and later updated by the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers (NACDL) reveals that twenty-one states, including Arkansas, Colorado, Utah, Nevada, Florida, New York, and Kansas allow some witnesses to have counsel present during grand jury proceedings. (NACDL, State by State Information Sheet¸ available at http://www.nacdl.org/grandjury. Furthermore, this proposed section of the measure appears to conform to the recommendations of the American Bar Association, put forth in a comment to a Judicial Advisory Committee of the Administrative Office of the United States Courts. Kansas additionally permits counsel to interpose objections. Calls for similar reform to allow witnesses the right to have counsel present during testimony have been echoed by the Cato Institute, the Capital Center for Government Law and Policy, and others

column1: The Association of California Life and Health Insurance Companies (ACLHIC), and the California Association of Health Plans (CAHP), write that similar policies have been attempted in other states without the desired results. For example, the OCCP was enacted by the Oregon state legislature during the 2013 session SB 604 (Anderson) of 2013. ACLHIC and CAHP write that the biggest concern is that this bill would prevent any healthcare entity from imposing additional criteria which may be determined based on quality or risk assessment. Further, there is also language that states, "This section does not prohibit a health care service plan or health insurer, or its delegated entity, from using another credentialing process or procedure." Plans presume this only comes into play if the provider does not want to use the certified credentialing entity. But it is not clear what would be allowed with this flexibility. Furthermore, allowing for more than one credentialing entity could lead to inconsistency. Providers could forum shop until they find an entity that will credential them. Even if these entities utilize the same standards, there is still likely to be inconsistency in credentialing decisions if there are different decision makers. Which regulatory body will ensure the credentialing entity covers all applicable credentialing criteria required? Will the board ensure that verification expiration dates are the same as other standards and basic credentialing requirements? Also, will the verifications be performed at the time of the request from a health plan? If the health plans are forced to accept the credentialing of an outside entity, will that entity bear the risk of a negligent credentialing action? Or will the plan be indemnified in some way? What about adverse providers (i.e. providers with quality issues, adverse actions, criminal records)? Who will determine the quality criteria for certifying adverse providers? Lastly, without a uniform database, how would plans obtain the provider data for these providers? What liability would providers be willing to assume for an accurate up to date database for streamlined credentialing
column2: Association of California Life and Health Insurance Companies;California Association of Health Plans

column1: The California Association of Health Plans, the Association of California Life and Health Insurance Companies, and America's Health Insurance Plans (collectively "opposition") write that drug manufacturers acknowledge their drugs are unaffordable for patients, but rather than choose to lower their prices for everyone, they point to their PAPs, which offer copay coupons. PAPs offer coupons only to a narrow set of patients, for a narrow selection of drugs, and often only for a limited time. Once the patient hits their deductible, drugmakers discontinue the patient's coupons. The opposition argues this scheme allows drugmakers to keep their underlying prices hidden from patients, while keeping their costs extremely high for employers and consumers who end up paying much more in premiums and cost-sharing. The opposition notes that the federal government considers copay coupons illegal kickbacks in federal programs like Medicare and Medicaid because these coupons induce a patient to use a specific drug. To counter the market manipulation from coupons, health plans and insurers have worked together with employers to develop programs to hold drug companies accountable, to shed light on these pricing schemes, and keep costs low for Californians. Such programs help restore the balance in the system by allowing patients to use manufacturer coupons to save money at the pharmacy counter, but does not count the amount the drug manufacturer has paid for the drug (through the coupon) towards the patient's deductible or OOP maximum. The opposition argues legislation like this bill that bans these programs by requiring health plans and insurers to count third-party payments towards an enrollee's cost sharing obligations will eliminate incentives for drug companies to lower prices. The opposition concludes that as a result, drug companies will make more money while California families and businesses continue to foot the bill through higher premiums, higher OOP expenses, and higher federal insurance subsidies

This bill would require firearms to be securely to the vehicle's frame using a steel cable lock or chain permanently affixed to the vehicle. In research conducted by the Alameda County District Attorney's Office, we discovered that between 2012 and 2017, law enforcement agencies across the state reported to the California Department of Justice, Automated Firearms System (AFS) 83,695 firearms stolen and 1,520 as lost. This data demonstrates that proper storage of firearms must be a high priority for our Legislature. Current law only mandates the proper storage of just a 'handgun' in an unattended vehicle. This bill would include all firearms including rifles, shotguns or assault weapons which are common types of weapons that are used by both law enforcement and law abiding citizens. Current law also does not address that if the handgun is locked in a container out of view, the whole container can be stolen. Current law also states that the handgun can be locked in the trunk but most trunks are easily accessible through the passenger compartment. This bill would additionally require the firearm to be secured to the vehicle's frame using a steel cable lock or chain that is permanently affixed to the vehicle
